overview.text: The Western Hognose Snake is a small, stout snake of the North American plains with an upturned, pig-like snout that it uses for digging. It is famous for its acting: when threatened it puffs up and hisses, and may even play dead.

identification.text: A short, thick body and an upturned nose scale. Its blotched pattern makes it look like a small rattlesnake, which may help keep enemies away.

size.label: Adults
size.text: Males are much smaller than females; adults rarely grow longer than about 40 to 50 cm.

distribution.label: Native
distribution.text: Southern Canada (Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba) south through the Great Plains of the United States to northern Mexico.

habitat.text: Sandy or gravelly ground: prairies, river floodplains, scrub, grassland and semi-desert, up to about 2,500 m.

behaviour.text: Active mostly by day. When threatened it flattens its neck like a cobra, hisses and makes 'bluff' strikes with its mouth closed; it almost never bites in defence. Hognose snakes may also roll over and play dead.

diet.text: Mostly frogs and toads, plus small lizards and the odd rodent. It is not a constrictor: it holds prey and works its rear teeth in.

reproduction.text: Lays 4 to 23 long, thin-shelled eggs in June to August; they hatch after about 60 days.

funfacts.text: When a hognose snake plays dead, it rolls on its back with its tongue hanging out!
